Addiction to opioids

Four small randomized trials reported reduced opioid craving after transcranial PBM. One trial also reported lower self-reported opioid use; retention and relapse outcomes remain less certain.

Summary of the Evidence

Nine publications are listed in the opioid-addiction category: six human publications, two animal experiments, and one review/overview. Four human publications are randomized trials; a fifth is a controlled quasi-experimental pilot cohort, and the sixth is a clinical case series. Across the randomized trials, short-term craving scores decreased after transcranial PBM. Two sham-controlled studies reported effect sizes of 0.73 and 1.5 for craving; one also reported a smaller effect size of 0.45 for self-reported opioid use. The estimated certainty is low-to-moderate for short-term craving reduction, low for opioid-use outcomes, and very low for treatment retention or relapse prevention.

Human and clinical evidence

Four randomized trials tested transcranial PBM. In a double-blind crossover trial of 22 adults, unilateral 810-nm LED treatment reduced craving more than sham, with a between-condition effect size of 0.73 (Schiffer et al. 2020). A separate two-site sham-controlled trial randomized 39 adults to eight treatments over four weeks. It reported an effect size of 1.5 for craving at the last follow-up and 0.45 for self-reported opioid use (Schiffer et al. 2021).

A 63-person randomized study compared 810-nm laser PBM, cognitive rehabilitation, and control over six weeks. Both interventions reduced craving versus control; PBM also performed better on working-memory and inhibitory-control measures (Hadadgar et al. 2024). A 70-person double-blind trial in people receiving methadone maintenance compared 810-nm LED PBM with sham and reported lower craving, anxiety, and depression scores through three-month follow-up (Helali et al. 2025).

A controlled quasi-experimental pilot cohort enrolled 50 people, of whom 39 completed the eight-week course. The PBM-plus-standard-care group reported lower craving and depression scores than the standard-care group (Flora and Huffer 2024). A 42-case clinical series described 382 treatments over 18 months; the clinician and patients rated responses as strikingly beneficial in 26 cases, helpful in eight, and not noticeable in eight (Schiffer 2021).

The category also includes one review/overview article on PBM across substance-use disorders, published as an “Insight” in Neuroscience Bulletin (Qin et al. 2026). The targeted opioid-indication search identified no systematic review or meta-analysis.

Animal evidence

One mouse and one rat experiment reported fewer naloxone-precipitated morphine-withdrawal signs after 830-nm laser exposure (Ojaghi et al. 2014; Mirzaii-Dizgah et al. 2009). These studies examine withdrawal responses in animal models.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No in-vitro or ex-vivo publication is classified in the opioid-addiction category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical studies used 810-nm near-infrared light delivered to the forehead with LED arrays, a wearable LED helmet, or a continuous-wave laser. Schiffer et al. used 250 mW/cm² for four minutes per exposure, reported as 60 J/cm² at the scalp and an estimated 2.1 J/cm² at brain level. The 2020 crossover study used three weekly visits; the 2021 trial used eight sessions over four weeks. Hadadgar et al. delivered laser light to 15–20 scalp points over 12 sessions in six weeks. Flora and Huffer used a 100-diode helmet for 16 sessions over eight weeks. Helali et al. reported four-minute exposures at both forehead sites, while the treatment-session schedule was not fully specified. The animal studies used 830-nm laser light.

Interpretation

The repeated clinical signal is a reduction in short-term opioid craving, with the largest reported estimates in two sham-controlled trials. One randomized trial also found a smaller reduction in self-reported opioid use. Current clinical publications provide limited information on retention, verified abstinence, and relapse prevention. Independent trials with longer follow-up and objective use outcomes can establish whether the craving changes are accompanied by sustained recovery outcomes.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Opioid craving — Schiffer et al. 2020 reported a between-condition effect size of 0.73 for active PBM versus sham. Schiffer et al. 2021 reported an effect size of 1.5 at the last follow-up.

Self-reported opioid use — Schiffer et al. 2021 reported an effect size of 0.45 on the Timeline Follow-Back measure.

Other randomized trials — Hadadgar et al. 2024 and Helali et al. 2025 reported statistically significant reductions in craving scores but their reports did not provide comparable standardized effect estimates.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term opioid craving reduction

Low for opioid-use outcomes

Very low for treatment retention and relapse prevention

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Four small randomized trials report lower opioid craving after transcranial PBM. One trial also reports a smaller reduction in self-reported opioid use. Confidence is limited by small samples, variation in protocols, and short follow-up. The pilot cohort and case series add clinical context; larger independent trials with objective use measures and longer follow-up would clarify whether craving changes translate into sustained recovery.
